subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Boston Tea Party Effect
description: A 60-second lesson on The Boston Tea Party Effect.

hook.text: In 1773, American colonists dumped tea in Boston Harbor. Drinking tea became unpatriotic overnight.

buildup.text: Colonists switched to coffee as an act of political defiance against British taxation and tea culture.

discovery.text: The Continental Congress declared coffee the official drink of the revolution. Taverns served it proudly.

twist.text: America's coffee habit wasn't about taste—it was a political identity that stuck for 250 years.

climax.text: Today the U.S. is the world's largest coffee importer, consuming 400 million cups daily.

punchline.text: A tea protest made America a coffee nation.

quiz.question: Why did American colonists switch from tea to coffee?
options: Drinking tea became unpatriotic after the Boston Tea Party

details.summary: When colonists dumped British tea in Boston Harbor in 1773, drinking coffee became a patriotic act. The Continental Congress endorsed coffee over tea. America's coffee culture was born from rebellion, and the preference for coffee over tea has defined American drinking habits ever since.
details.whyItMatters: The Boston Tea Party permanently shifted American beverage culture to coffee. Political protest created a national taste preference that persists 250 years later.
takeaways: The 1773 protest made coffee a patriotic alternative to tea
The Continental Congress endorsed coffee over tea
American coffee preference traces directly to this revolution

faq.question: How quickly did Americans switch from tea to coffee?
faq.answer: The transition was not instant but accelerated after 1773. Coffee consumption grew steadily through the Revolutionary era. By the early 1800s, coffee was firmly established as America's preferred daily drink, and tea never recovered its former dominance in the United States.

faq.question: Was coffee already popular in colonial America before the Tea Party?
faq.answer: Coffeehouses existed in major colonial cities like Boston, New York, and Philadelphia since the late 1600s. However, tea was more widely consumed in homes. The Tea Party gave coffee a political advantage and cultural identity that transformed it from an alternative to the default.
